name: Designing Solar for Coastal Fog and Shaded Hillside Homes in LA County

mainEntity.name: How does heavy coastal fog or hillside shading in parts of Los Angeles County affect my solar system design and panel choice?
mainEntity.text: How does heavy coastal fog or hillside shading in parts of Los Angeles County affect my solar system design and panel choice?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not all Los Angeles County roofs receive the same sunshine. Coastal neighborhoods often experience dense morning fog, while hillside and canyon homes can have shading from terrain and tall trees. These microclimate factors directly affect how much solar energy you can harvest and which technologies perform best. Coastal fog typically reduces early-day production; hillside shading can create complex, moving shadows that impact certain modules more than others. In such areas, standard production calculators based on generic “Los Angeles” sunshine can overestimate output. A proper site design should include a shade analysis with a tool like a solar pathfinder or digital app that accounts for both trees and local terrain. In many cases, higher-efficiency modules, microinverters, or DC optimizers can help reduce shading losses, although they may increase upfront cost. System layout also matters; installers may favor more east–west distribution or different stringing to smooth production and maximize usable energy under NEM 3.0. Before signing, ask for a shade report that clearly shows annual solar access percentage by roof plane and season. This lets you set realistic expectations, choose appropriate equipment, and decide whether tree trimming, ground mounts, or carport structures could significantly improve performance.
acceptedAnswer.description: Coastal fog and hillside shading in Los Angeles County reduce morning sun and increase partial shading, which impacts annual output and can justify higher-efficiency panels, more east–west strings, or module-level electronics. A site-specific shade study using local conditions is necessary before finalizing system size.
